title: The Watch in the Glove
markdown:
Leo disliked surprises. Leaves that rustled without warning. Quizzes that arrived like traps. Parties that were plots to make him look unprepared. His best days ran like a clock that had been wound on purpose.

Elara, his friend, was an apprentice watchmaker. She lived among gears that confessed their intentions. Order comforted her, the way a second hand comforts a minute.

They stood on the old platform at Oakhaven Station, where the timetable had given up being believed. Cobwebs made lace of the signs. A bench remembered more passengers than it currently hosted. The air held wet earth and a ghost of coal, and autumn leaves had made a small republic in the corner. A poster from 1928 still promised the Oakhaven Flyer to Willow Creek, on time, with cushions. Beside it a digital board blinked today’s date and a lost-package alert, as if two centuries had agreed to share a bench and not discuss politics.

Elara’s finger found a crack in the paper. “Same station. One almost a hundred years late.”

Leo leaned in. Special delivery, the old type said. Mr Silas Croft. Handle with great care. The modern alert named Silas Croft as well. The package: a pocket watch. Due today.

His stomach objected, on principle. Elara’s curiosity had the pull of a stream that knew its bed. “So both deliveries wanted the same man,” he said. “One lost. One still looking. A puzzle, then.”

Under the poster’s date a hurried smudge: 14 August 1928. Elara’s magnifying glass made a small sun of it. The poster kept a rhyme, odd as a joke left in a drawer: A stitch in time, a hasty rhyme, will see the treasure in its prime. Smaller still: If the conductor forgets his glove, the trunk holds more than just his love.

Leo’s dry laugh escaped. “What conductor forgets a glove? How does a trunk keep a watch?”

“A riddle,” Elara said, not sure. She lost polishing cloths the way other people lost trains. “Where has my little cloth flown? I say it, and I feel less foolish.”

At the far end of the platform sat a leather trunk, brass dim, handle travelled. It looked as if it had arrived with the station and never quite left.

“Silas Croft’s?” Leo offered.

“Conductors wore gloves,” Elara said. “They minded luggage. The glove is meant to say where. It only works if you get the joke.”

Leo’s mind, which usually locked the door on the unexpected, tried a different key. “Not forgetting. Finding, badly. A man in a hurry. Watch, tickets, gloves. He sets the watch down to fix his hat. He reaches for the gloves, still carrying too much, and the watch goes into a glove. The glove goes into the trunk. A silly public mistake. The sort people would have seen and smiled at, then forgotten.”

The air thinned, then tinted brown, like a photograph deciding to visit. A younger conductor hurried past, gloves in one hand, a crease of frustration between his eyes. He glanced back, opened the trunk, fumbled, left the lid a little honest, and was gone. The present returned, dusty and itself.

“The joke is the place,” Elara said. “Watch in the glove. Glove in the trunk.”

Leo walked to the trunk the way he walked to a pop quiz: unwilling, then curious despite himself. He lifted the lid. It complained, as old lids do. Among moth-eaten blankets that had once been someone’s winter, leather gloves lay as if they had been in a hurry and then forgotten the point. In the left one, something small and cool. He drew it out with the care Elara used for hairsprings. A pocket watch, silver cut with care, still ticking against his palm as if it had never been asked to stop. The second hand was a small, stubborn continuity.

They did not make a speech for the platform. Elara took the watch when he offered it, fingers fitting the case. “Where has my little cloth flown?” she said, and this time the line had a second person in it. They left. The station kept its coal-and-earth smell, and the two times on the wall went on not quite matching, which Leo, to his own surprise, found he could allow.
characters: Leo (boy who hates surprises), Elara (a watchmaker's apprentice)
audience: children aged 11-12, fantastic story for confident middle-grade readers
